claims.claim: In 2000, MIT physicist Seth Lloyd published a paper in *Nature* titled “Ultimate physical limits to computation.” The work calculated how much computation could be extracted from a kilogram of matter compressed into one liter, an imaginary machine that he dubbed the *ultimate laptop*.
claims.bestSource: How far can we push computing?
claims.evidence: In a 2000 paper in Nature titled “Ultimate physical limits to computation,” he worked out the answer and called the imaginary machine the ultimate laptop. Around the turn of the millennium, the MIT physicist Seth Lloyd took the question to its extreme: Imagine an ordinary lump of matter, a kilogram of it—about the mass of a laptop—packed into a liter of space.

claims.claim: Networks have always used edges to communicate with devices outside the core.
claims.bestSource: The world needs ever faster data processing. Edge computing will help - Mastercard
claims.evidence: Networks, by definition, have “edges” that can be used to communicate with machines and users outside the network itself, but now more computing is being done there — when we tap our cards to make a purchase or catch a train, or when we cruise through a tollbooth without tapping the brakes.

claims.claim: Today, more processing is occurring at those edges.
claims.bestSource: The world needs ever faster data processing. Edge computing will help - Mastercard
claims.evidence: The increasingly complex business of detecting and preventing fraud also makes a robust edge-computing strategy more vital than ever. Mastercard has stopped tens of billions of dollars in fraud using advanced techniques like machine learning, something no human or rules-based system could replicate. Pushing more of those advanced technologies close to the customer means a faster response based on more relevant data. The network started out processing payments for banks and retailers but has expanded into peer-to-peer transactions, digital identity verification, loyalty programs and security and fraud detection. This network has relied on edge computing from the start to cut down on response time, but also to add resiliency by creating backup pathways for data to flow through. For example, to enable public transit riders in London, New York and elsewhere to tap with their card from a mobile device or card, Mastercard worked with turnstile manufacturers to embed computing into the turnstiles themselves. That pushed much of the decision-making to the very edge, where riders are, instead of having the card data run all the way home to the network’s center and back again. The result is that riders know if their card is valid in less than a tenth of a second. For companies that run their own network, such as Mastercard, these shifts are profound — and also exciting, because they open new possibilities for ways to serve people around the world. In the past, someone swiping a debit card in a shop might have been willing to wait several seconds for the network to confirm a bank balance and run security protocols. Merchants, too, might not have expected to glean much information from that purchase, let alone get that intelligence delivered immediately. Enter edge computing, where more data flow and computation happen at the edges of a network instead of just in the center. Networks, by definition, have “edges” that can be used to communicate with machines and users outside the network itself, but now more computing is being done there — when we tap our cards to make a purchase or catch a train, or when we cruise through a tollbooth without tapping the brakes. The first is the shift from private to public (and hybrid) clouds. Public clouds are computing and storage for rent that enable businesses to scale up their services without having to build their own data centers. The other shift is the move to 5G wireless data networks, which dramatically speed up the ability to move data through the air to and from devices like smartphones. As more of our lives have shifted online, we’ve come to expect instantaneous service wherever we interact with a device, app or webpage. Merchants expect to understand their customers’ behavior in real time, and banks expect fraud and credit decisions to get smarter while happening faster. And with 5G and edge computing combined, cars and trucks driving along the tollway can make payments instantaneously. It’s constantly connecting to new devices — from smartphones to tiny sensors — and offering them more and more services, from e-commerce purchases to turnstile access at a subway. Think of how much data self-driving cars will require and how quickly they’ll need to make decisions. There’s just too much happening to rely solely on a central node for the kinds of technology — artificial intelligence, machine learning — that enables these innovations. Computing on the edge can make it happen in an instant.

editorial.claim: DARPA’s expansion signals that quantum technology is moving from theory toward practical benchmarks, though uncertainty remains about when it will mature.
Readers should watch how DARPA’s new awards shape the quantum landscape and monitor how edge‑computing technologies evolve in other sectors, from retail to transportation.
